title: The Church's clock
hook: psalms prayed at set hours around the world by priests, religious and laypeople

segments.voice: Yesterday, praying with imagination: stepping into Cana with all your senses. Your line was step into the story. Whose story did you step into? Today, not a scene but a clock, one that has been ticking for centuries. Day two hundred forty.

Right now, as you listen, somewhere on earth it's early morning, and in a monastery chapel a few sleepy monks are standing up to sing a psalm. Somewhere else it's evening, and a parish priest is opening a worn book at his kitchen table. Somewhere else a nurse on a night shift is reading the same psalm on her phone during her break. They've never met. They're praying the same words, set for the same day, on the same clock. The Church has a name for that clock. It's today's word.
screen: `A MONASTERY AT DAWN.` → `A PRIEST AT HIS KITCHEN TABLE.` → `A NURSE ON HER BREAK.`

segments.voice: First, the roots. Praying at set times of day is older than Christianity. The psalmist says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Seven times a day I have given praise to thee." The book of Daniel describes him praying three times a day toward Jerusalem. The Acts of the Apostles tells of Peter and John going up to the Temple at the hour of prayer, three in the afternoon. The first Christians kept the rhythm. Second, the monks. By the 500s, Saint Benedict organized his monks' days around these hours, and they prayed all one hundred fifty psalms every week. He called it the work of God. Nothing, he said, was to be put before it. For centuries this was mostly the prayer of monks, nuns and clergy, and people called it the Divine Office. Third, the hours today. After the Second Vatican Council, it was reshaped and published under the title Liturgy of the Hours, though many still call it the Divine Office, and the Church urged laypeople to pray it too, especially morning and evening prayer. The main hours are the Office of Readings, Morning Prayer, Daytime Prayer, Evening Prayer, and Night Prayer, which we'll meet tomorrow. Priests and deacons promise to pray it every day, and so do many religious. Each hour is mostly psalms, a short reading, a hymn and prayers. Fourth, the clock. Because the Church spans every time zone, as one place finishes evening prayer another is beginning morning prayer. The idea is that the whole Church, together, keeps the day holy, hour by hour. You don't pray it alone, even when you're alone. That's why your line is someone is always praying.
screen: `SEVEN TIMES A DAY: OLDER THAN THE CHURCH.` · `BENEDICT: THE WORK OF GOD.` · `MORNING, DAY, EVENING, NIGHT.` · `EVERY TIME ZONE, ONE PRAYER.` · then, large: `SEVEN TIMES A DAY I HAVE GIVEN PRAISE TO THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray one psalm at sunset, or sit with one. For now, settle and breathe, and let me give you one line that evening prayer has used for centuries, from Psalm 140: let my prayer be directed as incense in thy sight; the lifting up of my hands, as evening sacrifice. Picture the smoke of incense rising in a dark church. Picture hands lifted. Tonight at sunset, find that psalm, or any psalm, and read it slowly. If you pray, pray it. If you don't, read it knowing thousands are reading it too. The bell holds the time.
Liturgy of the Hours. The Church's daily prayer of psalms at set times, morning to night, prayed around the world. Today's word.
Your line: someone is always praying. Today, when you feel alone, remember that somewhere, right now, someone is praying a psalm for the whole world, you included. Day two hundred forty.

howItsDone: Catholic priests, deacons and many religious pray the Liturgy of the Hours daily, and a growing number of laypeople pray morning and evening prayer from a breviary or an app, alone or in parishes.

original.note: Latin: the Liturgy of the Hours, the name given after Vatican II.

trapdoor: what you thought: a prayer book for priests.
what it means: psalms prayed at set hours by the whole Church, in every time zone, so someone is always praying.
what a scholar hears: Benedict's opus Dei (Rule 43); reformed and commended to the laity by Sacrosanctum Concilium (1963), with the new Liturgia Horarum of 1971.

notes: Douay-Rheims Psalm 118:164 given from memory; confirm.

Psalm 140:2 is spoken in the practice without quotation marks from the Douay ('Let my prayer be directed as incense in thy sight; the lifting up of my hands, as evening sacrifice'); listed as a paraphrase source to be safe. Confirm wording; if exact, it may be marked as quoted.
Acts 3:1 'the ninth hour' = about 3 p.m.; Daniel 6:10 three times a day toward Jerusalem: confirm.
Benedict: all 150 psalms weekly (Rule ch. 18); 'nothing is to be put before the work of God' (ch. 43): paraphrased; confirm.

Obligation: priests and transitional deacons promise to pray the Hours; permanent deacons per their conference; religious per their constitutions. Simplified to 'priests and deacons promise'. Confirm.
The new Liturgia Horarum typical edition 1971 (promulgated 1970): confirm.

Reviewer softened 'given a new name' to 'published under the title Liturgy of the Hours, though many still call it the Divine Office' (the older name remains in official use), and 'opened to the laity' to 'commended to the laity' (lay recitation was never barred).
